data.text:
**Claim 0: CO at 400 ppm. Supported as written.**
- AICO says "400 ppm – frontal headaches within 1-2 hours. These CO levels become life-threatening if exposed for longer than 3 hours." https://www.aico.co.uk/homeowner/articles/carbon-monoxide-levels-explained/
- FireAngel says that at 400 ppm, frontal headaches can develop within 1-2 hours, and exposure becomes life-threatening after about three hours. https://www.fireangel.co.uk/homeowners/support/what-symptoms-do-you-get-at-different-carbon-monoxide-co-ppm-levels/
- Kidde gives the same figures: frontal headaches within one to two hours at 400 ppm. https://www.kidde.com/support/carbon-monoxide-alarms/co-levels-info
- Superior, WI (a municipal government page) is slightly different. It lists 400 ppm as "Headache and nausea after 1-2 hours of exposure." https://www.superiorwi.gov/1089/Carbon-Monoxide-Alarms
- Caveat: these are alarm makers and a city page. The figures are rough guides, and the 3-hour line comes from the manufacturers, not a medical source. Kidde also says a 400 ppm alarm sounds in 4 to 15 minutes. That is the alarm's response time, not the symptom time.

**Claim 1: Chimney height. Supported as written.**
- The "3-2-10 rule" is that the chimney must rise "at least 3 feet above where it passes through the roof, and stand at least 2 feet taller than anything within 10 feet of it." https://www.flue-pipes.com/us/info/required-height_of_a_chimney
- The same manufacturer says NFPA 211 sets this rule. https://www.flue-pipes.com/us/info/chimney-pipes-building-codes
- Chimney Insight says IRC section R1003.9 mirrors NFPA 211: 3 ft above the roof at the point of penetration and at least 2 ft above any structure within a 10-foot horizontal radius. https://chimneyinsight.com/chimney-height-calculator-roof-obstruction-rules/
- Caveat: I found no copy of the NFPA 211 text itself. These are secondary sources quoting it. Local codes and the stove maker's installation instructions may be stricter.

**Claim 2: Wood cookstove oven at about 230 °C (450 °F). Supported in a corrected form.**
- I found no engineering or manufacturer source giving a typical wood cookstove oven temperature. The sources I found cover ovens in general, and wood-fired pizza and masonry ovens.
- Wikipedia's "Oven temperatures" lists a "Hot oven" at 400–450 °F (200–230 °C) and a "Very hot oven" at 450–500 °F (230–260 °C). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oven_temperatures
- Conversion: 450 °F is 232.2 °C, usually written as 230 °C (gas mark 8). https://kitchenconvert.io/convert/450-f-to-c
- Wood-fired oven guides give 400–450 °F (200–230 °C) for bread and general baking. https://chicagobrickoven.com/blogs/the-hangout/what-temperature-should-a-wood-fired-pizza-oven-be-a-simple-guide-for-beginners
- Corrected form: "A wood cookstove oven can reach a hot baking temperature of around 230 °C (450 °F)." Or say "can be brought up to." A wood stove has no thermostat, so the temperature depends on the fire. Typical baking runs from about 175 °C to 230 °C (350–450 °F). The 230 °C figure is the top of the hot-oven range, not a fixed value.

**Claim 3: French "cuisinière". Supported as written.**
- Wiktionary lists two senses. One is "cook," the "female equivalent of cuisinier." The other is "stove, range" (kitchen appliance). The word comes from *cuisine* + *-ière*. https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/cuisini%C3%A8re
- Dictionary.com defines it as "a female cook or chef." https://www.dictionary.com/browse/cuisiniere
- French Today says: "Une cuisinière = a female cook but also a stove top, a range." https://frenchtoday.com/blog/french-vocabulary/how-to-say-to-cook-in-french-cuir-cuisiner-faire-la-cuisine
- Caveat: Wiktionary also glosses the appliance as "cooker." That is the British word for a stove.
